column3: Nucleor could not read the requested source file.
column4: The compiler could not open or read the input file. This is usually a path, permission, or working-directory problem rather than a language error.
column5: Verify the file path passed to the command.Check file permissions and current working directory.If using a package, confirm [build].entry points to an existing file.

column3: A use target or package import could not be resolved safely.
column4: The import graph could not be resolved because a target was missing, escaped its package boundary, created a cycle, or conflicted with another exported symbol.
column5: Check the imported path or package alias.Ensure the import stays inside the package root.Look for duplicate exported names or cyclic imports.

column3: The lexer found an invalid character or token shape.
column4: The source text cannot be tokenized into valid Nucleor tokens. This usually means a malformed literal, a non-ASCII identifier, or an unexpected character.
column5: Check the reported source offset for the invalid character.Verify string and numeric literal syntax.Keep identifiers ASCII-only.

column3: The token stream does not form valid Nucleor syntax.
column4: The parser reached a token sequence that does not match the grammar. This is usually a missing delimiter, malformed declaration, or invalid expression shape.
column5: Check the line and column around the reported span.Look for missing braces, commas, semicolons, or parentheses.Verify declaration headers and function signatures.

column3: A `let` statement initializer was not terminated by `;`, so the next token would otherwise be parsed as a separate expression statement.
column4: Nucleor requires `let name: Type = expr;` or `let name = expr;`. Pre-v1.1 builds could accept input such as `let x: i64 = 1 2 3;` and silently drop the trailing tokens as no-op expression statements. The parser now rejects the statement before lowering or codegen.
column5: Add `;` immediately after the let initializer.If another value follows the initializer, connect it with an explicit operator or split it into a separate statement.Re-run the build and check the first token named after the reported byte offset.

column3: The program parsed, but semantic typing rules were violated.
column4: The checker rejected the program because types, names, effects, or ownership rules did not line up. More specific semantic failures use narrower codes when possible.
column5: Read the concrete message for the exact mismatch.Check variable names, function signatures, and return types.Use nuc explain on any more specific code shown with the diagnostic.

column2: Borrow Safety Failure (legacy — superseded by RFC-0062 G-series at v1.0)
column3: Ownership or borrowing rules were violated. (Legacy code — at v1.0 the modern compiler emits the specific RFC-0062 G-series codes instead: OWN-G4-USE-AFTER-DROP, OWN-G8-COND-MOVE, BORROW-G2-LIFETIME, ALIAS-G3-VEC-OF-REFS, ALIAS-G3-HASHMAP-REHASH, INIT-G11-READ-BEFORE-INIT, SEND-G6-* — see `nuc explain <CODE>` for any of those.)
column4: The checker found an illegal aliasing, move, or borrow pattern. Typical causes are moving a borrowed value, mixing shared and mutable borrows, or using a value after move.
column5: Check whether the value was moved earlier in the scope.Avoid overlapping shared and mutable borrows.Introduce a narrower scope so the borrow ends before the next use.

column3: A denied effect, purity rule, or policy restriction was violated.
column4: The program attempted an operation that the current effect context, purity contract, or active policy block does not allow.
column5: Check the function effect list and current restricts or policy context.Add the required effect only if the operation is intentionally impure.If the operation must stay pure, refactor the side effect out of the function.

column3: Tainted data reached a location that requires trusted input.
column4: The taint system prevented untrusted data from flowing into a sink that expects sanitized or trusted values.
column5: Identify the tainted source in the data flow.Sanitize or validate the value before the sink.Keep tainted and trusted values separated until validation is complete.

column3: A spawned or shared context captured a type that is not safe to transfer or share.
column4: The checker found a cross-thread or cross-scope capture that violates Nucleor's Send/Share rules. This usually means a resource, mutable reference, or other non-Send value crossed a spawn boundary.
column5: Move only owned Send values into spawn blocks.Avoid capturing mutable references across thread boundaries.Wrap shared state in a synchronization primitive only when the underlying payload is allowed.

column2: Explicit enum discriminants not yet supported
column3: Explicit enum discriminants `enum X { A = N }` are not yet supported in v0.6 — the parser halts at the `=` token.
column4: v0.6.35 — closes probe finding 2026-05-01-enum-discriminant-segfaults-compiler. Workaround: drop the `= N` and rely on order-based discriminants (`enum Code { OK, WARN, ERR }` lowers to 0, 1, 2). For FFI / wire-protocol values needing specific numbers, build a separate `const` table. Real explicit-discriminant lowering is forward-roadmap (needs the enum AST to carry per-variant i64 values + IR-emit propagation to match-arm dispatch).

column2: Self-recursive struct without Box / & indirection (Rust E0072)
column3: A struct that contains itself directly (`struct Node { next: Node }`) has infinite size — Rust E0072. Wrap the recursive field in `Box<Node>` (heap indirection), `Option<Box<Node>>` (linked-list / tree shape with terminator), or `&Node` (reference) so the field is a fixed size.
column4: v0.6.36 — closes probe finding 2026-05-01-self-recursive-struct-infinite-size-accepted. Pre-fix `struct Node { val: i64, next: Node }` was accepted at parse + type-check and crashed at instantiation with STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW (Windows exception 0xC00000FD) — the struct contains itself directly so the size is infinite. v0.6.36 catches it at parse-time. Wrap the recursive field in `Box<Node>` / `Option<Box<Node>>` / `&Node` so the field is a fixed size. Real recursive-struct lowering through Box is already supported; only the bare-recursion case needs the halt.

column3: The typed AST could not be lowered into compiler IR.
column4: Lowering hit an internal semantic boundary the IR pipeline could not represent. This is usually a compiler implementation gap rather than a front-end syntax issue.
column5: Look at the full message for the unsupported construct.Reduce the program to the smallest failing example.Treat repeated NR040 failures as compiler bugs to fix in lowering.

column3: IR generation succeeded, but a backend could not emit valid target code.
column4: LLVM rejected the IR, hit an unsupported ABI path, or failed during object emission or linking preparation. (R10-D6 v0.8.278: removed 'Cranelift or' — Nucleor ships only the LLVM backend; no Cranelift backend exists. Phase 2 may add Cranelift as a tier-0 fast-path; until then docs and diagnostics must not imply a backend that's not there.)
column5: Re-run with the other backend to isolate whether the failure is backend-specific.Check the reported symbol or ABI path in the message.Treat verifier or emission failures as backend correctness bugs.

column3: WASM output was requested without the required backend support.
column4: The current CLI build does not include the backend support required for wasm code generation, or the wasm linker/toolchain is unavailable.
column5: Rebuild the CLI with backend support required for wasm enabled.Install or point NUCLEOR_WASM_LD at a working wasm-ld.Confirm the LLVM toolchain is visible in PATH.

column3: Project metadata, dependency graph, or lockfile state is invalid.
column4: Nucleor could not resolve the project package graph because the manifest was malformed, a dependency could not be found, or the lockfile was missing or stale.
column5: Validate Nucleor.toml syntax and dependency paths.Run nuc lock after manifest changes.Check workspace member and dependency graph cycles.

column3: An internal compiler stage received invalid state from a previous pass.
column4: A compiler pipeline stage ran out of order or consumed data that was not produced by the earlier stage it depends on. This is an internal compiler bug, not a user program error.
column5: Reduce the failing program to a small reproducer.Treat repeated NR090 failures as compiler bugs.Inspect the named pipeline stage and previous stage outputs.

column3: A #[no_alloc] function called something that allocates from the global heap.
column4: RFC-0001 #[no_alloc] forbids any expression whose effect set includes alloc. Common offenders: Box::new, Vec::push past capacity, String operations, HashMap::insert. Use a pre-sized container, an arena/pool/tlsf allocator (RFC-0002), or refactor the allocation outside the RT path.

column3: A #[no_panic] function contains an expression the compiler cannot prove is panic-free.
column4: RFC-0001 #[no_panic] uses a conservative dataflow analysis. Sources of panic include integer overflow on +/-/*, division by zero, out-of-bounds indexing, unwrap() on Option/Result, and explicit panic!(). Use checked_*/wrapping_*/saturating_* arithmetic, guard divisions, use get() instead of [], and prove safety with assume! (RFC-0004).

column3: A #[no_dyn] function uses dynamic (vtable) dispatch via dyn Trait.
column4: RFC-0001 #[no_dyn] forbids dynamic dispatch via Box<dyn Trait> or &dyn Trait. Replace with generics (fn f<T: Trait>(x: T)) for static dispatch, or with an enum-based polymorphism pattern.

column2: Heuristic deadline estimate exceeds declared #[deadline] (NOT certified WCET)
column3: A HEURISTIC compile-time estimator (statement-counter + coarse loop multiplier) flags this function as likely to exceed its declared #[deadline]. RT-004 is NOT certified WCET — it does not model callee cost, ISA, cache, or branch prediction. Use #[allow(RT-004)] / #[allow_fn(RT-004)] when the estimate is wrong; treat the runtime deadline check as the actual contract. Certified WCET is future work (RFC-0001 §Heuristic vs certified WCET).
column4: RFC-0009 static WCET analysis estimates the function's worst-case time exceeds the deadline. Inspect the dominant cost in the report; reduce loop bounds, simplify hot paths, or relax the deadline if appropriate.

column2: FFI call in RT function without #[ffi_no_*] annotation
column3: An RT-tagged function called an extern fn lacking #[ffi_no_alloc] or #[ffi_no_panic].
column4: Calls into C/C++ via extern fn are opaque to the analysis. Mark trusted extern declarations with #[ffi_no_alloc] and/or #[ffi_no_panic] (v0.3.24, RFC-0001 §3.5) -- two separate attributes, not one comma-list. #[deadline] callers need BOTH markers (intersection rule). To skip per-symbol annotation: #[allow(RT-005)] (file-wide).

column3: RT attributes (#[no_alloc], #[deadline] etc.) cannot be applied to async fn — async semantics break the deadline guarantee.
column4: async fn introduces poll-based scheduling and arbitrary suspend points. RT attributes promise bounded time and no allocation; the two are fundamentally incompatible. Refactor the function as sync, or use rod/tokio (RFC-0030) outside the RT path.

column2: `async` keyword on fn is silently stripped (v0.5 has no Future/.await; use async_spawn + async_await for threading)
column3: Pre-v0.5.19 `async fn foo() { ... }` was silently stripped to `fn foo()` and ran sync immediately. Adopters writing the canonical Rust async pattern got immediate execution with no signal. Nucleor v0.5 has no Future / .await polling; threading is via `async_spawn(fn_ptr, arg)` + `async_await(handle)` (RFC-0027 phase 1). Either drop the `async` keyword for sync fns, or call `async_spawn` to actually thread.
column4: Workaround: drop the `async` keyword if you want sync execution (the keyword was a no-op pre-v0.5.19, now triggers this warning). For real threading, use `async_spawn(fn_ptr, arg)` to spawn the fn on an OS thread → returns an opaque task handle. Then `async_await(handle)` joins the thread and returns the captured i64 result. See stdlib/rods/async.nr and the RFC-0027 phase 1 commitment to threads-only (no green-thread scheduler, no future polling).

column2: Deadline annotation without no_alloc or no_panic
column3: A #[deadline] annotation alone is incomplete — it is hard to reason about deadline without #[no_alloc] or #[no_panic].
column4: Add #[no_alloc] or #[no_panic] (or both) to the fn -- that makes the deadline reasoning sound. To intentionally suppress: #[allow(RT-007)] (file-wide) or #[allow_fn(RT-007)] (per-fn, v0.3.20). The warning surfaces a likely-incomplete annotation.

column3: A #[deadline] function uses recursion. Bound it with #[max_depth = N] (RFC-0014).
column4: Deadline analysis cannot bound an unbounded recursion. Annotate the function with #[max_depth = N] per RFC-0014 to give the analyzer a depth bound.

column3: A #[no_panic] function contains an integer `/` or `%` operator. Integer divide/modulo panic when the divisor is zero. Phase 1 (v0.8.295) flags this as a warning because the estimator does not yet prove non-zero divisors at the IR level. Suppress with `#[allow_fn(RT-009)]` when the divisor is provably non-zero, or replace with `checked_div` / `checked_rem` for explicit Result-typed handling. Phase 2 (R03-D2) adds IR-level non-zero proof.
column4: Rust's `#[no_panic]` (via the `no_panic` crate) checks at link time. Nucleor checks at build time. The integer-divide-by-zero case is a known gap in Rust's checker too — RT-009 surfaces it explicitly so adopters can decide.

column3: An #[allow(_fn)(CODE)] or #[deny(_fn)(CODE)] attribute references a CODE that is not in the canonical enumerated diagnostic code set. The suppression or promotion has no effect at compile time -- the diagnostic the author meant to control still fires unsuppressed. Catches both unknown-prefix codes (e.g. WAT-001) and within-series typos (e.g. RT-099 vs RT-009).
column4: v0.3.38 enumerated check: the s1 compiler validates the full CODE substring against the canonical diagnostic code set (mirrored in cli_explain_full_smoke). When minting a new code, add to BOTH the s1 compiler's is_known_diag_code fn AND the cli_explain_full_smoke codes array. To suppress DIAG-001 itself during a noisy refactor: #[allow(DIAG-001)].

column3: A value allocated in an arena/pool/tlsf cannot outlive its allocator. The borrow checker rejects returning the value when the allocator goes out of scope.
column4: Per RFC-0002, Box<T, A: Allocator> is bound by the lifetime of A. Returning a Box<T, Arena> from a fn whose Arena is local is rejected. Either pass &Arena into the fn (caller owns the arena), or copy the value into a Box<T, Global> before returning.

column3: Two values from different allocator types cannot be combined where one is required.
column4: Allocator type is part of the value type. fn f(x: Box<T, Arena>) cannot accept a Box<T, Pool>. Use generics (fn f<A: Allocator>(x: Box<T, A>)) for allocator-agnostic APIs.

column3: An allocation site reaches a #[no_alloc(...)] context that forbids that allocator.
column4: RFC-0001 #[no_alloc(...)] accepts an explicit allow-list of allowed allocators. The default #[no_alloc] forbids all four (global/arena/pool/tlsf); narrow with #[no_alloc(global)] etc.

column2: Cannot add values in different coordinate frames
column3: Spatial values in different coordinate frames cannot be combined directly. Transform via tf.lookup or apply an explicit Transform.
column4: RFC-0003 typed frames make Pose<World> != Pose<BaseLink> at the type level. To combine, look up the transform: tf.lookup::<World, BaseLink>(time).apply(pose_world).

column3: Transform<A, B> * Transform<C, D> requires B == C. The compiler rejected the composition.
column4: Transform composition Transform<A,B> * Transform<C,D> requires B == C. The compiler enforces the chain at compile time. Reorder, invert one transform, or look up an intermediate.

column2: Cannot apply transform to value in incompatible frame
column3: Transform<A, B>.apply(Pose<C>) requires C == A. The compiler rejected the application.
column4: Applying a Transform<From, To> requires the target value to be in the From frame. Convert via lookup of the appropriate transform.

column3: A value was moved into another binding or call; using the original now would alias freed/owned memory. Clone before the move, or restructure to avoid the second use.
column4: Borrow-checker classic: a value was moved (consumed) into a struct, fn argument, or another binding. Subsequent reads of the original would alias freed memory. Fix: clone the value before the move (if `T: Clone` is satisfied), restructure to take a reference, or sequence the code so the original isn't read after the move. The compiler shows the move site and the use site.

column3: Cannot create a new borrow of a value that has been moved. The borrow target no longer exists at the source's binding.
column4: OWN-002 fires when you try to *borrow* a value that was previously moved. The borrow target no longer exists at the source binding (the value has moved elsewhere). Same fix as OWN-001 — clone or restructure.

column2: Cannot move value that is borrowed
column3: A move would invalidate an outstanding borrow. Wait for the borrow to end (typically by ending the borrowed-reference's scope) before moving.
column4: Move-while-borrowed: an outstanding `&T` or `&mut T` would dangle if the source moves. The compiler tracks active borrows and rejects moves that would invalidate them. Sequence so the borrow ends before the move (typically by ending the borrow's lexical scope).

column2: Cannot mutably borrow value already borrowed
column3: Two simultaneous mutable borrows would alias. Sequence the borrows or use interior mutability via Atomic<T> for cross-thread sharing.
column4: Two simultaneous `&mut T` of the same value would alias mutable memory — Nucleor (like Rust) forbids this at compile time. Sequence the borrows so they don't overlap, or use Atomic<T> / per-thread split for genuine cross-thread sharing.

column3: A shared (immutable) borrow cannot coexist with a live mutable borrow — would risk reading partially-mutated state. End the mutable borrow first.
column4: Cannot create `&T` while `&mut T` of the same value is live — the shared reader could observe the mutator mid-update. Drop the mutable borrow first, then take the shared one.

column3: Shared references (`&T`) are read-only by construction. Use `&mut T` if you need to assign through the reference.
column4: `&T` is read-only by definition. Trying to assign through it is a category error. Either change the binding to `&mut T` (which requires the source to be `let mut`), or use Cell/RefCell for interior mutability (with the runtime borrow-tracking cost).

column3: Mutating a location that is currently borrowed (directly or via a struct-field reachable through the borrow) would invalidate the borrow. End the borrow first.
column4: Assigning to a location that is currently borrowed (or whose enclosing struct is borrowed) would invalidate the borrow — the borrowed value would disappear or change underneath the borrow holder. Drop the borrow first.

column3: The binding was declared `let x` (immutable). Use `let mut x` to allow assignment after the initial bind.
column4: `let x` declares an immutable binding; subsequent `x = ...` is rejected. Use `let mut x` to make the binding mutable. (Note: `let mut x = 5; let x = x + 1;` is also valid — the second `let` shadows the first as a new binding.)

column2: Cannot return reference to local value
column3: The function would return a reference to a stack-local value; the value's storage is freed at function exit so the reference would dangle. Return by value or take/return a reference with a longer-lived source.
column4: Returning `&local` from a function returns a reference to stack memory that's freed at function exit. Either return the value by-move (which transfers ownership), allocate on the heap and return Box<T>, or take a `&mut Out` parameter and write into it.

column2: Cannot bind a reference that escapes an inner block
column3: A reference's source value lives in a nested scope that ends before the binding's scope; the reference would dangle. Move the source out to the enclosing scope, or hold the source by value at the outer scope.
column4: Inner-block lifetime escape: `let r = { let x = 5; &x };` would leave `r` pointing at freed `x`. The compiler tracks scope-exit destruction and rejects bindings that would outlive their referent. Move the source value out to the outer scope, or hold by value rather than reference.

column3: `&mut T` requires the source to be declared `let mut x`. Make the binding mutable, or restructure to take a shared `&T` instead.
column4: `&mut T` requires the source to be declared `let mut`. Add `mut` to the binding, or use `&T` if you don't actually need to write through the reference.

column2: Cannot destroy arena with live references
column3: An arena cannot be destroyed while references into it are still live — would dangle every outstanding pointer. End all borrows from the arena before destroy.
column4: Arenas free all their backing storage on destroy. If any reference into the arena is still live, the destroy would dangle every outstanding pointer. End all borrows from the arena (typically by exiting the scope where they live) before destroy.

column2: Spawn block captures non-Send DeviceBuffer value
column3: GPU `DeviceBuffer` handles are pinned to the thread that allocated them, so they are not `Send`. A `spawn { ... }` block runs on a fresh thread and cannot capture them. Move the launch into the owning thread, or pass a host-side handle that the worker can re-acquire its own DeviceBuffer from.
column4: Spawn-capture pass detected a `spawn { ... }` block capturing a `DeviceBuffer` value. GPU memory handles are pinned to the thread that allocated them via the CUDA / Vulkan context binding — the worker thread that spawn dispatches to has no context attached, so the capture would be undefined behavior at runtime. Either keep the launch on the owning thread (process the buffer there before spawning the consumer), or pass a host-side handle (CPU-side index / descriptor) that the worker re-acquires its own DeviceBuffer from with its own context.

column2: Non-Sendable value crosses a spawned boundary
column3: RFC-0035 requires values moved into spawned work to be Sendable. Primitive values, Sendable containers, and types with an explicit `impl Sendable for T` pass this first check.
column4: Add an explicit `impl Sendable for T {}` when the type is safe to move across tasks, or keep the value on the originating thread.

column3: Actor calls can suspend on the actor executor. Calling them without await would bypass the serialization contract.
column4: Await actor method calls so the actor executor serializes access.

column3: Actor fields are isolated mutable state. Direct field access from outside the actor bypasses the actor executor and is rejected.
column4: Expose actor state through an actor method instead of reading or assigning fields directly.

column2: Shared mutable state without Mutex or actor
column3: Shared mutable state needs an actor or synchronization primitive so two tasks cannot mutate it concurrently.
column4: Wrap shared mutable payloads in an actor or an audited synchronization primitive.

column3: A mutable reference crossing a thread boundary can outlive the source stack frame or race the original owner. Move owned data or use synchronization.
column4: Do not pass `&mut T` to spawn/thread APIs; move an owned Sendable value or pass a synchronized handle.

column3: The same actor lock cannot be re-entered while already held; doing so can deadlock or violate serialized state access.
column4: Refactor the actor method to avoid re-entering the same actor while its lock is held.

column2: Deadline composition under actor await is invalid
column3: Deadline checking and actor await composition require a scheduler-aware bound. The first pass rejects the combination.
column4: Move the actor await out of the deadline region or use scheduler-aware actor latency tooling when it lands.

column2: #[not_sendable] type used where Sendable is required
column3: `#[not_sendable]` is an explicit opt-out from structural Sendable inference. The compiler honors it even when fields look safe.
column4: Remove `#[not_sendable]` only if the type is genuinely thread-safe; otherwise keep it out of spawned work.

column3: Reserved for a future RFC-0035 Sendable/actor diagnostic.
column4: Reserved diagnostic; no user action.

column3: Reserved for a future RFC-0035 Sendable/actor diagnostic.
column4: Reserved diagnostic; no user action.

column3: The source declares `@policy(require_authored)` at the module level but at least one function lacks an `@authored(\"name\")` annotation. Add `@authored(\"...\")` to every fn, or remove the policy.
column4: The `@policy(require_authored)` module-level attribute requires every fn in the source to carry an `@authored(\"name\")` annotation (the governance audit trail). The audit pass found at least one un-annotated fn. Add `@authored(\"...\")` above each fn, or remove the policy if it doesn't apply to this module.

column3: The source declares `@policy(no_unsafe)` at the module level but contains an `unsafe { ... }` block. Either remove the unsafe block (preferred) or remove the no_unsafe policy.
column4: The `@policy(no_unsafe)` module-level attribute forbids `unsafe { ... }` blocks anywhere in the source. The audit pass found at least one. Either remove the unsafe block (preferred — usually means switching to a safe API) or remove the no_unsafe policy if the module legitimately needs unsafe operations.

column2: Tainted data passed to sensitive sink
column3: Tainted data flowing into a function annotated as a sensitive sink. Wrap the value in `sanitize(value)` to strip the taint marker before the call.
column4: Strict-mode taint pass detected tainted data flowing into a function annotated as a sensitive sink. The suggestion is to wrap the value in `sanitize(value)` (which strips the taint marker) before the call. Fires from the tools-suite strict checker, not the s1 main type-check pass.

column2: Non-exhaustive match (LEGACY — unified under MATCH-001 in v0.5.18; no longer emitted)
column3: Legacy non-exhaustive-match warning. Unified under the canonical MATCH-001 (RFC-0016) in v0.5.18 — TYP-001 is no longer emitted by the main compiler (was always paired with MATCH-001 with identical text; the dual-emit was a noisy adopter UX hazard). The explain entry stays so existing adopter docs / scripts that reference TYP-001 still resolve.
column4: **Legacy** non-exhaustive-match warning. Unified under the canonical MATCH-001 (RFC-0016) in v0.5.18. The main compiler no longer emits TYP-001; only MATCH-001 fires (with identical text). The explain entry stays so existing docs that reference TYP-001 still resolve to a meaningful description.

column2: Boolean values cannot be used in arithmetic
column3: Booleans are not numeric in Nucleor; `true + false` etc. are rejected. Use `if cond { 1 } else { 0 }` if you need to convert.
column4: Booleans aren't numeric — `true + false`, `bool * bool`, etc. are rejected. The arithmetic operator type-check (in check_expr's binop branch) fires TYP-002 when either operand resolves to bool.

column2: Unit operands for addition/subtraction must match
column3: RFC-0005 — adding two unit values requires identical dimensions (both must be `unit<T,m>` or both `unit<T,s>`, etc.). Convert one to the other or use multiplication.
column4: RFC-0005 — adding `unit<T,m>` and `unit<T,s>` is dimensionally invalid (length-plus-time has no physical meaning). Convert one to the other via the appropriate physical relationship, or use multiplication (`unit<T,m> * unit<T,1/s>` produces `unit<T,m/s>`).

column3: The `*` (deref) operator only applies to `&T` / `&mut T` / `Box<T>`. Applying it to a value type (`i64`, struct field by value, etc.) is rejected.
column4: The `*` (deref) operator is defined only on `&T`, `&mut T`, and `Box<T>`. Applying it to a value type, struct field by value, or i64/f64 is a category error — those are already values, not references to values.

column3: The call site supplies a different number of arguments than the function declared. Check the function signature.
column4: Argument arity mismatch. The function declares N parameters; the call site passed M ≠ N. Check the function signature and the call site. Variadic dispatch isn't supported in v0.2.

column3: Argument N has a type incompatible with parameter N's declared type. Includes taint-marker type mismatches (passing tainted T to a clean T parameter).
column4: Argument N has type incompatible with parameter N's declared type. Includes the taint-marker case: passing `T tainted` to a parameter declared as plain `T` (or vice-versa) fires TYP-006 rather than a separate TAINT-* code.

column2: Bare numeric literal cannot initialize a unit value
column3: RFC-0005 unit values must be initialized via the unit constructor (e.g. `meters(5.0)`) — a bare `5.0` doesn't carry the dimension tag and would silently mix units.
column4: RFC-0005 unit values must be initialized via the unit constructor (e.g. `meters(5.0)`, not `5.0` alone). A bare numeric literal doesn't carry the dimension tag and would silently mix units when assigned to a `unit<...>` binding.

column3: `let x: T = expr` requires `expr` to type-check as `T`. Mismatched types produce TYP-008 with the expected and actual types.
column4: `let x: T = expr` requires `expr` to type-check as `T` (or coerce per the type lattice in RFC-0015 §3). Includes taint-marker mismatches between the declared type and the expression's type.

column3: `x = expr` requires `expr` to match `x`'s declared type after the initial bind. Re-binding to a different type isn't allowed without a fresh `let` shadowing.
column4: After the initial bind, `x = expr` requires `expr` to match `x`'s declared type. Re-binding to a different type isn't allowed without a fresh `let` shadowing (which creates a new binding rather than re-typing the existing one).

column3: `return expr` requires `expr` to type-check as the function's declared return type. The body type and the signature type must agree.
column4: `return expr` (or implicit tail-expression return) requires `expr` to type-check as the function's declared `-> T`. Body type and signature type must agree.

column3: `str + str` (and longer chains like `\"a\" + \"b\" + \"c\"`) silently SIGSEGVed pre-v0.4.51 because the binop lowered to i64_add on the string pointers, producing a garbage pointer that crashed in print_str. Use `str_concat(a, b)` to concatenate strings.
column4: Nucleor's i64-everywhere ABI lowers `+` to integer addition. For `str + str` that meant adding two string pointers as i64, producing a garbage pointer that SIGSEGVed when later passed to a string helper (e.g. `print_str`). Pre-v0.4.51 this was silent at compile time. v0.4.51 promotes the pattern to a hard error pointing at `str_concat(a, b)`. Reasoning: the canonical Rust idiom `&str + &str` doesn't compile in Rust either, so adopters expected a compile error and got runtime garbage instead.

column2: Missing field(s) in struct initialization (would silently default to 0/empty)
column3: Pre-v0.4.62 `Point { x: 1, y: 2 }` for a struct with 3 fields silently defaulted the missing field to 0 / empty. Adopters writing the canonical Rust idiom (which errors with E0063) got a quiet wrong value. Either list every field explicitly or define a `Point::new(x, y)` constructor fn that supplies the rest.
column4: Struct constructor expressions like `Point { x: 1, y: 2 }` must list ALL declared fields. Pre-v0.4.62 the lower silently zero-initialized any missing field — equivalent to a quiet `field: 0` (or `field: \"\"` for str). Rust errors here with E0063, so adopters writing the canonical idiom got a wrong value with no compile-time signal. Workaround: list every field explicitly, OR write a `Point::new(x, y)` constructor fn that supplies the rest.

column2: Unknown field in struct initialization (would silently drop the extra field)
column3: Pre-v0.4.63 `Point { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }` for a 2-field Point silently dropped the extra `z` field (Rust E0560 errors). Check the struct definition and remove the unknown field, or add it to the struct decl.
column4: Pre-v0.4.63 `Point { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }` for a 2-field Point silently dropped the extra field — the lower walked the init list in declared order, so any extra entries past the declared count were ignored. Rust errors here with E0560 — adopters writing canonical struct literals got a quiet wrong shape. Either remove the unknown field from the literal, or add it to the struct definition.

column2: Invalid or unproven `as char`, or non-void function reaches the end without returning a value
column3: `as char` requires a valid Unicode scalar value. Constant casts must be within 0..0x10FFFF and outside 0xD800..0xDFFF; non-constant casts must be guarded by a recognized scalar-range proof such as `v >= 0 && v < 0xD800`. This code also covers non-void functions that can fall through without an explicit return or tail expression.
column4: For `as char`, keep invalid constants out of the cast and guard dynamic codepoints before casting. For missing returns, audit every control-flow path and make the returned value explicit; side-effect-only functions should return void.

column3: Strict inference mode found an expression whose type checker returned the empty-type sentinel. The compiler rejects it instead of treating the unknown type as compatible with every annotated type.
column4: Add a concrete type annotation or route the expression through a helper whose return type is known to the type checker. For collection helpers, prefer typed methods or explicit wrappers until strict inference becomes the default.

column2: Implicit integer width conversion in binding
column3: A binding annotated with one integer width was initialized by another integer width. Silent widening or narrowing is rejected so portability and truncation are explicit.
column4: Cast explicitly with `as` at the binding site, or change the annotation to the expression's real integer width.

column2: Type does not implement Display for bare `{}` formatting
column3: Bare `{}` formatting for a user struct requires an `impl Display for Type` with `fn fmt(self) -> str`; use `{:?}` for derived structural debug output.
column4: `println!(\"{}\", value)` previously fell through to `int_to_str(value)` for struct values, printing an ABI handle instead of user-facing text. The format expander now hard-errors unless the struct has a Display impl; `println!(\"{:?}\", value)` remains the structural debug path.

column2: Format string has more arguments than `{}` placeholders (extras would be silently dropped)
column3: `format!(\"{}\", 1, 2, 3)` (more args than placeholders) silently dropped the extras pre-v0.5.11 — including any side effects in the dropped argument expressions. Either add `{}` placeholders for each extra arg or remove the unused args from the call. Mirrors the v0.4.70 placeholder>args check (the loud-direction asymmetry that left this case silent).
column4: Pre-v0.5.11 `format!(\"just {}\", 1, 2, 3)` silently dropped args 2 and 3 — the format expander walked the placeholders and stopped at the first arg, leaving the rest unevaluated/unreferenced. Adopter typos (left an arg after removing a placeholder) and refactor mistakes (renamed a placeholder, kept the arg) hit silently. v0.5.11 mirrors the v0.4.70 placeholder>args check direction so both asymmetries halt cleanly. Side-effecting expressions in dropped args (e.g. `format!(\"{}\", 1, expensive_call())`) no longer evaluate-then-discard.

column2: Missing From conversion for `?` error propagation
column3: `?` on `Result<T, SrcErr>` inside a function returning `Result<U, DstErr>` requires `impl From<SrcErr> for DstErr` when the error payload types differ.
column4: The `?` operator propagates the Err payload early. When the callee error type and enclosing function error type differ, Nucleor now performs the Rust-style `From<SrcErr> for DstErr` conversion. If that impl is absent, continuing would either return the wrong payload layout or silently expose the source error type through the destination API, so the compiler stops with TRAIT-001.

column3: Nucleor follows Rust's no-implicit-conversion rule. Cast explicitly with `as`: `(u8_val as i32) + i32_val`.
column4: Nucleor models on Rust: numeric types are distinct, no implicit conversion. Cast explicitly with `as`. Reasoning: silent conversions are a recurring bug source (truncation, sign extension).

column2: Numeric literal out of range for declared type
column3: The literal does not fit in the declared type — e.g. 256u8 overflows u8.
column4: Numeric literal exceeds the declared type's range — e.g. 256u8, -1u32, 4_000_000_000i32. Use a wider type or change the literal.

column3: An `as` cast may truncate or round. The warning is informational; promote to error with #![deny(precision_loss)].
column4: Casting f64 to i32, i64 to i8 etc. may lose precision or wrap. The warning surfaces the risk; if intentional, suppress with #[allow(precision_loss)] on the call site.

column3: The current target lacks hardware support for the requested low-precision float (f8e4m3 / f8e5m2 / f16 / bf16); the operation is emulated in software and may be slow.
column4: RFC-0015 §3.4 — f8e4m3 / f8e5m2 (NVIDIA Hopper formats), f16 (IEEE half), and bf16 (Brain float) need hardware support to be fast. Without it the operation is emulated via f32 conversion in the runtime. The warning is informational; suppress with #[allow(no_hw_lp_float)] or move the kernel to a target that has the instruction set.

column3: usize and isize are platform-pointer-width and incompatible with explicit i64 / u64 etc. without cast.
column4: usize/isize represent platform-pointer-width values used for indices and pointer arithmetic. Mixing with explicit i64/u64 risks portability bugs across 32-/64-bit targets.

column3: Signed and unsigned of the same width are distinct types. Cast one explicitly: `(u32_val as i32) + i32_val`. Reason: silent sign-coercion is a recurring bug source in C/C++.
column4: Signed and unsigned types of the same width are distinct. Cast explicitly to make the conversion intent visible at the call site. Storage is i64-uniform under the hood, but the type system enforces sign-discipline.

column2: Float→int cast saturates to type bounds
column3: Float→int cast saturates to the target's max/min when the value is out of range (matches Rust). Use `.try_as_i32()` if you want a Result-typed conversion that surfaces overflow.
column4: Float→int cast in Rust semantics saturates (3e9 as i32 = i32::MAX, NaN as i32 = 0). Catches the silent-truncation bug class C inherits from its float→int rules.

column2: Shift amount equals or exceeds operand width (UB-prone)
column3: Shift amount must be < operand width. `let x: u8 = 1; let y = x << 8;` is UB in C, returns 0 in some Rust modes, traps in others. Nucleor matches Rust 'wrapping shift' semantics in release; debug builds trap.
column4: Shifting by >= the operand width is UB in C and panics in Rust debug mode. Nucleor matches Rust's release-mode wrapping shift; debug-mode trap will land with #[overflow(trap)] phase 7.2.

column3: A function annotated `@const_fn` contains an effectful operation (I/O, allocation, panic-capable expression, or ambient capability). const-fns must be pure so they can be evaluated at compile time. Either remove the @const_fn annotation, or move the effectful work to a separate normal fn. Audit R09-D4 (NUM-G9) v0.8.293 — pre-v0.8.293 @const_fn was silently ignored; post-v0.8.293 it's enforced fail-closed.
column4: C/C++ has no compile-time-evaluation contract; Rust's `const fn` enforces purity at the type-checker level. Nucleor's @const_fn now matches Rust: if the body could run effects at runtime, it can't be evaluated at compile time, so it's rejected. Phase 2 will actually evaluate and fold pure const_fn bodies.

column3: Router-level: --tier <X> got a value other than 0/1/2. Phase 2 wires --tier through to clang -O level + cache key + artifact metadata.
column4: Tier validation lives at the router (powershell wrapper) so the compiler is never invoked with a malformed --tier; Phase 2 wires the value through. This matches Rust's split between `cargo` and `rustc` flag validation.

column3: A function annotated `@hot` contains a perf-violation: heap allocation (Vec::new / Box::new) or I/O (print / println / panic). Hot paths should be alloc-free and I/O-free; either suppress with #[allow_fn(PERF-2)] when intentional, or move the work out of the @hot body. Audit R10-D2 v0.8.297 — pre-v0.8.297 @hot was discovery-only; post-v0.8.297 violations emit a warning.
column4: C++ has no `@hot` annotation; profile-guided optimization is the closest analogue. Rust's `#[inline(always)]` is a hint, not a contract. Nucleor's @hot is checker-enforced (Phase 1 warning, Phase 2 will promote some violations to error).

column2: Heap allocation inside a while/loop block (HeapInLoop)
column3: A function body contains a Vec::new() or Box::new() call inside a `while` or `loop {}` block. Per-iteration heap allocation is the dominant perf bug class for adopters who compose with std collections. Move the alloc outside the loop (`let mut v = Vec::with_capacity(n);` then push inside), or use a stack buffer, or `#[allow_fn(PERF-3)]` when intentional. Audit R10-D2 v0.8.298.
column4: Rust's clippy has the `needless_collect` lint and similar; this PERF-3 is the simpler ancestor — just don't allocate per iteration. C++ relies on profilers to catch this; Nucleor surfaces it at compile time.

column2: Implicit narrowing of f64 literal to f32 may lose precision
column3: An f64 literal assigned to an f32 binding is narrowed via `__nucleor_as_f32` at the bind site (Phase 5). For most literals this is exact; for values requiring more than 24 bits of mantissa precision (e.g. 0.1), the rounded f32 differs from the f64.
column4: f64 → f32 narrowing rounds to nearest representable f32, which is exact for many literals (1.0, 0.5, 2.5) but loses precision on others (0.1, 1/3). The warning is informational.

column2: Overflow attribute conflicts with operation kind
column3: `#[overflow(trap)]` on a function whose body uses `wrapping_add` is contradictory — wrapping_add is opt-in and won't trap regardless of the attribute. Pick one mode.
column4: #[overflow(trap)] + wrapping_add inside the same fn produces inconsistent semantics — wrapping always wraps regardless of attribute. Refactor to use the matching primitive.

column2: Cast from pointer to non-pointer-width integer
column3: Casting `*const T` or `*mut T` to a non-pointer-width int (i8/i16/i32) loses bits on 64-bit targets. Use `usize`/`isize` for round-trip-safe pointer-int conversions.
column4: Pointer-int cast portability: 32-bit targets have 32-bit pointers; 64-bit targets have 64-bit pointers. Use usize/isize for round-trip safety; explicit i32/i64 risks losing bits on the wrong target.

column3: `Vec<T>` requires T to be a primitive or sized struct. Generic / trait-object element types are not yet supported (lands with the Vec<T> monomorphization phase).
column4: Vec<T> monomorphization (Phase 8) currently supports primitives + flat structs. Generic / trait-object element types need a vtable layer that lands later.

column3: `sizeof_struct(Foo)` requires Foo to be a defined struct with non-generic field types. Phase 3b ships byte sizes for primitives + simple structs; nested generic structs land in 3b.2.
column4: sizeof_struct is compile-time-constant; the struct must be statically known. Generic struct parameters (Vec<T> field of an outer struct) defer to runtime via a separate sizeof query.

column2: extern fn signature uses non-ABI-stable type
column3: `extern fn` signatures should use ABI-stable C types: i8..i64 / u8..u64 / f32 / f64 / ptr / str. Nucleor-only types (Vec<T>, str, generics) are forwarded as i64 handles via FFI but won't link to native C.
column4: ABI stability matters when other languages call into Nucleor-compiled libraries. Stick to the C-stable types; Vec / str / generics need a manual marshalling layer.

column2: Comparison between signed and unsigned of equal width
column3: Comparing i32 < u32 risks sign mismatch — the negative i32 is interpreted as a giant u32. Cast one operand explicitly to make the intent visible.
column4: Equal-width sign mismatch is the C 'comparing -1 to 0xFFFFFFFF' bug — the comparison silently sign-extends and yields wrong answers. Always cast first.

column2: Bitwise op on signed type may have surprising sign-extension
column3: Bitwise ops on signed types preserve the sign bit on right shift (arithmetic shift). For unsigned semantics use `bit_shift_right` (logical); for sign-preserving use `bit_shift_right_signed`.
column4: Right-shift on a signed integer preserves the sign bit (arithmetic shift). For -8 >> 1, you get -4 (arithmetic) or 0x7FFF...FC (logical). Pick the helper matching your intent.

column3: A float literal (`3.14`) was used where an integer is expected. Either cast (`3.14 as i32`) or change the binding type to f32/f64.
column4: Integer context expects an integer; a float literal there is almost always a typo. If you intended a truncating conversion, write it explicitly with `as`.

column2: Negative literal assigned to unsigned type
column3: `let x: u8 = -1` doesn't fit in u8 (range 0..255). Use `255u8` (the wrap result) or change the type to i8 / i16.
column4: Unsigned types can't represent negative values. -1u32 as a literal is rejected; (-1 as u32) compiles and gives u32::MAX (the wrap result).

column3: `let a: i32 = 5; let b: i64 = 6; if a < b { ... }` mixes widths. Cast one operand: `if (a as i64) < b { ... }`.
column4: Mixed-width comparison forces a widening conversion. Make it explicit so the reader sees which operand is being widened and why.

column2: Integer literal or constant expression overflows at compile time
column3: A decimal integer literal exceeds u64::MAX, or a module-level const integer expression overflows i64 during compile-time evaluation. Pre-fix these paths wrapped through compiler internals and either produced meaningless bits, runtime-startup panics, or confusing generated-IR failures.
column4: For oversized literals, reduce the literal or use a wide-int library. For const expressions, use an explicit wrapping_* / saturating_* helper, reduce the value, or move the calculation to runtime if wrapping is intentional.

column2: Integer vs float in arithmetic/comparison binop
column3: `5 < 5.0` mixes integer and float operands; pre-v0.4.137 this silently coerced and the comparison produced unexpected results. Cast one operand: `5.0 < 5.0` or `5 < (5.0 as i64)`.
column4: Pre-v0.4.137 the compiler silently coerced int↔float at binop sites; user programs got wrong results because LLVM's fcmp on bit-cast operands compares bit patterns, not values. NUM-022 turns the silent miscompute into a compile-time error so the cast intent is explicit.

column3: `(3.14 as str)` and `(true as str)` are not defined as numeric `as`-casts. Use `str_from_float` / `str_from_bool` (or format) instead.
column4: `as` is for numeric truncation/extension. `f64 as str` and `bool as str` were silent no-ops that returned an undefined pointer (URGENT — could SIGSEGV). NUM-023 rejects the cast and points at `str_from_float` / `str_from_bool`.

column2: Cross-width call-site narrowing audit (opt-in via NUCLEOR_AUDIT_NUM024=1)
column3: Opt-in audit warning. With `NUCLEOR_AUDIT_NUM024=1` set, the compiler reports every call site where a wider-typed argument flows into a narrower-typed param via Nucleor's i64-everywhere ABI. v0.4.230 closed the audit surface to 0/0 across self-build by widening str_from_int's signature; the audit remains as a regression gate.
column4: Audit-only. Nucleor's call ABI forwards every value as i64 regardless of the param's declared type. v0.4.221's attempt to trunc-on-entry broke the compiler's self-build because `str_from_int(n: i32)` was called with i64 magnitudes; v0.4.230 widened that signature and the audit surface dropped to 0/0. NUM-024 is now a permanent regression gate — any new declared-iN param called with a wider source-level type fires the warning.

column3: The match does not cover all variants of the matched type. The compiler shows a witness uncovered value.
column4: The match must cover every variant of the discriminant type, or use a wildcard (_) arm. Compiler shows the missing case.

column3: An arm is preceded by patterns that already match every case it would handle.
column4: Patterns are tested in order. A later arm cannot match if an earlier arm covers all values it would handle.

column3: Match arm bodies must produce the same type (or () in statement context).
column4: All arms in a match expression must yield the same type. Cast or restructure to align.

column2: ? in a function not returning Result/Option
column3: The ? operator desugars to a function-level early return; the function must return Result/Option for ? to type-check.
column4: The ? operator desugars to `match e { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => return Err(e) }`. The function must return Result (or Option for option-?) for the desugar to type-check.

column2: ? error type doesn't Into the function's error type
column3: ? converts the inner error via `From::from`. The compiler cannot find an impl mapping the source error type to the function's declared error type.
column4: RFC-0016 §3.7 — implement `From<SourceError> for TargetError` (or use a single boxed error type). The ? desugar inserts the conversion automatically.

column3: unwrap() panics on Err/None. Use unwrap_or, ?, or match in #[no_panic] code.
column4: Use unwrap_or, unwrap_or_else, ?, or match in #[no_panic] context. The compiler treats unwrap as may_panic.

column2: Range pattern bounds in wrong order
column3: Range patterns like `1..=5` require `low <= high`. The compiler refuses inverted bounds since they would never match.
column4: RFC-0023 §3.1 — swap the bounds. Half-open ranges `1..5` exclude the upper bound and have the same restriction.

column3: Or-patterns like `Some(x) | Other(x)` must bind the same set of names with the same types in every arm so the body type-checks identically.
column4: RFC-0023 §3.2 — every alternative must bind the same names with compatible types. Restructure the patterns so each path produces an identical binding set.

column3: Slice patterns split a slice into prefix/middle/suffix. Two patterns claiming the same element are ambiguous and rejected.
column4: RFC-0023 §3.4 — at most one wildcard prefix/middle/suffix per slice pattern. Restructure to a non-overlapping decomposition.

column3: An @-binding (e.g. `n @ 1..=5`) introduces a fresh name; using a name already in scope is rejected to prevent silent shadowing.
column4: RFC-0023 §3.3 — pick a fresh identifier for the binding, or `let outer = outer;` to make shadowing explicit before the match.

column2: Match arms produce values of incompatible types
column3: Every arm of a match expression must yield the same concrete type (or unit `()` in statement context). Pre-v0.4.140 heterogeneous arms silently produced whichever value the runtime hit first, with the wrong type stored in the result slot — a runtime SIGSEGV class.
column4: RFC-0023 §3.5 — restructure each arm to yield the same type. Use a common ancestor (often `i64`) or split the match into kind-specific branches that don't merge.

column2: Struct pattern field after `:` must be an identifier (literal field-equality patterns deferred)
column3: Struct patterns currently support only the binding form `Point { x, y }` and the rename form `Point { x: rename, y: rename }`. Field-equality literal patterns like `Point { x: 0, y: 0 }` are deferred to v0.5+. Express the same intent today with a guard: `Point { x, y } if x == 0 && y == 0 => ...`. Pre-v0.4.163 the parser fed the literal's raw value as a string-id binding, producing garbage that crashed codegen with an ACCESS VIOLATION.
column4: RFC-0023 §3.6 — replace `Point { x: 0, y: 0 }` with `Point { x, y } if x == 0 && y == 0 => ...`. Field-equality literal patterns ship in v0.5+ once nested-pattern lowering is wired.

column2: Float scrutinee or float-literal pattern in `match` is not supported
column3: Float scrutinees (`match x { ... }` for x: f32/f64) and float-literal patterns (`1.5 => ...`) are not supported. Float equality is fragile: NaN ≠ NaN, and arithmetic round-off makes literal-equality unreliable. Pre-v0.4.206 the compiler crashed with ACCESS_VIOLATION (no diagnostic) on float-lit patterns or float-typed scrutinees. Use an `if`-chain with tolerance (`if (x - 1.5).abs() < 0.001 { ... }`) or convert via `(x * 100.0) as i32` to match on integer scaled values.
column4: Float pattern matching is intentionally unsupported (NaN ≠ NaN; round-off drift). Use an `if`-chain with tolerance, OR convert the float to a scaled integer (`(x * 100.0) as i32`) and match on the integer. Pre-v0.4.206 the compiler crashed with ACCESS_VIOLATION on this construct; now halts with a clear MATCH-013.

column2: Negative literal bounds in range patterns are not yet supported
column3: Range patterns currently parse only non-negative integer literal bounds. A pattern such as `-10..=-1` tokenizes as unary minus plus integer literal at each bound, and that unary form is not part of the range-pattern grammar yet. The compiler now halts with MATCH-014 instead of falling through to the generic NR020 expected-token error.
column4: Use a guard today: `_ if value >= -10 && value <= -1 => ...`, or shift the matched domain before matching so the range bounds are non-negative literals. Full negative-bound range parsing needs unary-minus support in pattern grammar.

column2: Negative literal pattern in match arm not yet supported
column3: Negative literal patterns (`-5 => ...`) are not yet parsed; the unary minus is read as an operator, not part of the literal pattern. Sister to MATCH-014's range-bound limitation. Use a guard for now: `_ if x == -5 => ...`.
column4: Use a guard today: `_ if x == -5 => ...`. Full negative literal pattern parsing ships alongside MATCH-014's range-bound fix.

column2: Cross-enum pattern: scrutinee enum type does not match constructor's enum type
column3: A pattern's enum constructor (e.g. `Color::Red`) names a different enum type than the scrutinee. Pre-v1.0.1 (Lane 1 audit fix F-002) this miscompiled silently — `match a { B::On => ... }` for `a: A` would lower the B variant tag against A's vtable, returning whichever A variant happened to share the tag value. The check now fires when the scrutinee's enum type can be inferred.
column4: Either name the matching enum constructor (e.g. `A::Red` for a scrutinee of type `A`) or restructure to dispatch over the actual scrutinee enum. Lane 1 audit close (F-002) wires the structural check; the diagnostic is gated on the type-checker having scrut_t populated for the match site.

column3: The assume! predicate uses an expression form the analyzer doesn't track for static reasoning. Runtime check still happens; static benefit is none.
column4: RFC-0004 §3.2 lists the predicate vocabulary the analyzer understands: x < N, x != 0, arr.len() == N, opt.is_some(), result.is_ok(), equality substitution. Other predicates are accepted as runtime checks but contribute nothing to static analysis.

column3: assume_unchecked! disables even the debug-mode runtime check. The warning surfaces a missing comment justifying the unsafety.
column4: RFC-0004 §3.6 — assume_unchecked! is a footgun for extreme RT loops. Document why the runtime check is too costly to justify.

column3: The assume! predicate is true for all inputs (e.g., assume!(x == x) or assume!(true)). The runtime check is dead code; remove the assertion.
column4: RFC-0004 §3.9 — the compiler simplified the predicate to TRUE; the assume! adds no information for the analyzer and the runtime check is dead code. Delete the assume!.

column3: The assume! predicate is provably false from the type system (e.g., assume!(x < 0) for x: u32).
column4: The compiler proved the predicate is unsatisfiable at this program point. The assume! is wrong.

column3: In --profile=cert, every assume! must be discharged via SMT proof or explicit chain-of-trust. The verifier could neither prove nor refute this one.
column4: RFC-0004 §3.1 — in --profile=cert every assume! must be discharged. The proof obligation goes to the SMT pipeline; if neither prove nor refute is reached the cert build fails. Add a justification comment, derive the predicate from a stronger fact in scope, or weaken the assume.

column3: Adding/subtracting unit<T,m> and unit<T,s> is dimensionally invalid. Convert one to the other or use multiplication.
column4: RFC-0005 §3.1 — units form a 7-dimensional polynomial. Add/sub require equal dimensions; mul/div produce sums/differences of dimension exponents.

column3: Implicit unit conversion is forbidden by RFC-0005. Use explicit .into() or From::from to cross unit systems.
column4: RFC-0005 §3.4 — silent unit conversions are exactly the bug class typed units exist to prevent.

column2: Power expression is non-integer at compile time
column3: Unit exponents must resolve to integers at compile time. e.g. m^2 is fine but m^x where x is runtime is not.
column4: RFC-0005 §3.1 — unit exponents must be compile-time integer constants (positive or negative). Runtime-computed powers don't form a valid unit type. Refactor to use a fixed exponent or wrap in a dimensionless helper.

column3: Unknown unit alias. Check stdlib/rods/units_si.nr or units_imperial.nr.
column4: RFC-0005 §3.3 — alias library lives in stdlib/rods/units_si.nr (SI), units_imperial.nr, units_robotics.nr.

column3: An @law annotation references quantities whose unit dimensions don't reduce — e.g. claiming a force-times-time equals a length.
column4: RFC-0005 — @law annotations carry through unit checking. If the LHS and RHS of the law reduce to different unit dimensions the law is dimensionally wrong; review the law's algebra.

column3: A #[require(...)] precondition was violated by the caller. Caller must satisfy the predicate before the call.
column4: RFC-0006 §3.2 — #[require] is checked at the call site (debug profile) or assumed (release). Either fix the call or relax the require.

column3: A #[ensure(...)] postcondition was violated by the function body. Body must produce a result matching the predicate.
column4: RFC-0006 §3.3 — #[ensure] is checked at function exit. The function returned a value or modified state in a way that violated the contract.

column3: A #[invariant(...)] struct invariant was violated on method entry or exit.
column4: RFC-0006 §3.4 — invariants checked on entry to + exit from every public method. Either restore the invariant before the method ends or weaken the invariant.

column3: Liskov substitution: a trait impl cannot weaken the trait's preconditions. Add the missing #[require] to the impl.
column4: RFC-0006 §3.5 — Liskov substitution principle. Trait impls cannot weaken preconditions; the impl must satisfy at least the trait's #[require].

column3: Liskov substitution: a trait impl cannot strengthen the trait's postconditions either. The impl must guarantee at least what the trait promised.
column4: RFC-0006 §3.5 — the dual of CONTRACT-004. An impl that promises strictly more than the trait breaks substitutability when callers swap the impl through a trait object. Match the trait's #[ensure] verbatim or weaken.

column2: old(expr) references mutable state without snapshot
column3: old(expr) reads the value at function entry; if expr was mutated by the body, take an explicit snapshot at entry first.
column4: RFC-0006 §3.3 — old(expr) snapshots the value at function entry. If expr was mutated by the body, old(...) sees the post-mutation value because no entry snapshot was taken. Capture explicitly: `let _entry_x = x; ... old(x) = _entry_x;`.

column2: In cert profile, contract not statically provable
column3: In --profile=cert, every contract must be statically discharged. The SMT backend could not prove the predicate; tighten or annotate.
column4: RFC-0006 — in --profile=cert, every contract is SMT-discharged. The solver could not prove the predicate. Strengthen the require/ensure with an additional clause that closes the gap, or annotate `#[contract(approximate)]` to fall back to runtime check.

column3: A #[ensure(...)] predicate references result, but the annotated function returns no value.
column4: Remove `result` from the ensure predicate, or give the function a concrete return type if the contract is meant to constrain the returned value.

column3: NUCLEOR_DBC_MODE must be one of debug, safe-release, release, or cert.
column4: Unset NUCLEOR_DBC_MODE for debug behavior, or set it explicitly to debug, safe-release, release, or cert.

column3: old(...) snapshots function-entry state and is only meaningful in postconditions, not preconditions.
column4: Move the old(...) check into #[ensure(...)] or compare directly against the incoming parameter in #[require(...)].

column3: A contract predicate references an identifier that is not a fn parameter, DbC keyword (true/false/null/Some/None/Ok/Err/result/old/self), CamelCase type or variant name, or fn call site.
column4: Check spelling of the identifier; rewrite the predicate to compare against a fn parameter; or qualify with a path / fn-call / field-access if it's actually a module-level reference.

column3: #[atomic] functions cannot block. Mutex::lock, Channel::recv, sleep, or syscalls are forbidden. Use lock-free structures (SpscQueue, MpmcQueue) or Atomic<T>.
column4: RFC-0007 §3.3 — #[atomic] is the inter-thread RT contract. Use Atomic<T> ops, SpscQueue/MpmcQueue.try_push/try_pop, and avoid all blocking primitives.

column3: #[atomic] implies #[no_alloc]. See RT-001 explanation.
Cell/RefCell carry runtime borrow checks that can panic; #[atomic] forbids panicking control flow. Use Atomic<T> primitives instead.
column4: RFC-0007 — Cell/RefCell rely on runtime borrow tracking that may panic; #[atomic] forbids panicking flow because it would break atomicity guarantees. Replace with Atomic<T> or AtomicCell<T>.

column3: compare_exchange takes (success, failure) orderings; failure must not be stronger than success and not Release/AcqRel. The compiler enforces the ordering lattice.
column4: RFC-0007 §3.2 — compare_exchange takes (success_ordering, failure_ordering); failure cannot be stronger than success and cannot be Release/AcqRel (since failure does not perform a write). Compiler enforces the ordering lattice as defined by the C++/Rust memory model.

column2: Invalid memory ordering for atomic load/store
column3: atomic_load accepts Relaxed, Acquire, or SeqCst. atomic_store accepts Relaxed, Release, or SeqCst. Acquire stores and Release loads are invalid memory-model combinations.
column4: RFC-0007 §3.2 maps MemOrder to LLVM atomic ordering keywords. LLVM rejects release/acq_rel loads and acquire/acq_rel stores; use Acquire/SeqCst for loads and Release/SeqCst for stores.

column2: Atomic helper inside closure is temporarily unsupported
column3: Closure lowering does not yet inherit the parent function's enum-variant scope for atomic memory-order constants.
column4: Call the atomic helper directly from a regular function body instead of wrapping it in a closure until closure scope inheritance lands.

column3: An ISR is entered by hardware, so the first pass accepts only a zero-argument void function. Move data exchange through atomics or static state.
column4: RFC-0008 first pass — hardware-entered handlers must be `fn() -> void` with no params and no return value.

column3: Deadline wrappers measure wall-time function calls. ISR latency is target interrupt timing, so #[deadline] composition is rejected.
column4: RFC-0008 first pass — `#[isr]` rejects `#[deadline]`; use ISR-specific latency/vector tooling instead of deadline wrappers.

column3: The current ISR lowering substrate recognizes cortex-m4f and rv32imac. Other targets must wait for a target-specific interrupt ABI ship.
column4: RFC-0008 first pass — target-specific interrupt calling conventions are enabled only for cortex-m4f and rv32imac; other targets fail closed.

column2: Vector name not recognized for target
column3: The vector name in #[isr(vector = ...)] does not match this target's PAC. Check stdlib/embedded/<target>/vectors.nr for the valid set.
column4: RFC-0008 §3.1 — vector names are target-specific. The PAC for your MCU is in stdlib/embedded/<target>/vectors.nr.

column2: Two ISRs assigned to the same vector
column3: Two #[isr] functions claim the same vector. The vector table can only bind one — combine them or distinguish the priorities.
column4: RFC-0008 §3.3 — the vector table maps each interrupt source to exactly one handler. Two #[isr]'s claiming the same vector is ambiguous; either combine them, or use a software dispatch shim.

column2: Priority out of range for target NVIC
column3: Cortex-M NVIC priorities range 0..2^N where N depends on the chip (typically 3–4). The supplied priority is out of range.
column4: RFC-0008 §3.1 — Cortex-M NVIC priority bit-width varies (typically 3 or 4 bits = 8 or 16 priority levels). Check stdlib/embedded/<target>/nvic.nr for your chip's priority range.

column2: Malformed prio attribute (negative / string / missing value)
column3: The `prio` named attribute inside #[isr(prio = N)] requires a non-negative integer literal. Pre-v0.6.32 negative-int / string-literal / bare-ident were silently accepted with undefined effect on the target controller.
column4: v0.6.32 — `#[isr(prio = N)]` requires N to be a non-negative integer literal. Pre-fix the prio attribute parser silently accepted negative-int (`-1`), string-literal (`\"high\"`), and missing-value (bare `prio`) shapes; v0.6.32 catches them at the attribute site.

column3: #[isr] is meaningful only on fn items. Pre-v0.6.31 it was silently dropped on non-fn items (struct/enum/impl/trait/mod/use/const/static/type) AND leaked to the next fn, surfacing as a misleading ISR-001 diag pointing at the wrong fn.
column4: v0.6.31 — `#[isr]` may only be applied to fn items. Pre-fix the attribute was silently dropped on non-fn items AND leaked to the next fn in the file, producing a misleading ISR-001 diag pointing at the wrong fn (typically `main`). Originally shipped under ISR-004; renamed to ISR-008 in v0.6.32 because ISR-004 is reserved for the planned 'vector name not recognized' diag (RFC-0008 §3.1).

column3: Heptane needs a static call graph; dyn Trait or fn-pointers without #[wcet_dispatch_table] make targets unknown. Make the dispatch concrete or annotate the table.
column4: RFC-0009 §3.5 — Heptane needs a static call graph. dyn Trait or fn-pointer dispatch makes the callee unknown. Either rewrite as monomorphized static dispatch or annotate with #[wcet_dispatch_table(...)] listing the candidate targets.

column3: Add #[loop_bound(N)] or assume!(arr.len() == N) so Heptane can bound the loop.
column4: RFC-0009 §3.2 — Heptane needs trip counts to bound loops. Annotate the loop with #[loop_bound(N)] or assert the array length with assume!(arr.len() == N) before entering.

column3: Static WCET upper bound exceeds the declared deadline. See the WCET report for the dominant cost path.
column4: RFC-0009 §3.3 — static WCET upper bound exceeds the declared deadline. The diagnostic shows the dominant cost path. Reduce loop bounds, simplify hot expressions, or relax the deadline.

column3: Indirect call (function pointer / closure) without a declared dispatch table — Heptane cannot bound the callee. Annotate or rewrite as static dispatch.
column4: RFC-0009 §3.5 — same root cause as WCET-001 but specifically for fn pointers stored in a struct field or passed as an argument. Provide a #[wcet_dispatch_table] for the fn-pointer site.

column3: Recursion in the WCET graph exceeds the #[max_depth] bound. Either raise the bound or refactor to iteration.
column4: RFC-0009 + RFC-0014 — Heptane unrolls recursive calls up to #[max_depth]; if the analysis exceeds the bound, raise it (paying for the WCET cost) or eliminate the recursion.

column3: Heptane crashed or returned an internal error. File a bug with the IL dump from `nuc dump --wcet-il`.
column4: RFC-0009 — internal Heptane error. Re-run with `nuc dump --wcet-il -o /tmp/wcet.il` and file a bug attaching the IL dump.

column3: DLPack tensor's device kind doesn't map to any device this Nucleor build supports. Check the supported set with `nuc target list`.
column4: RFC-0010 §3.3 — DLPack defines device kinds (1=CPU, 2=CUDA, 3=CPUPinned, 4=OpenCL, ...). Nucleor binds the subset its target supports. Re-export with kind=1 (CPU) or recompile against a target that includes the device.

column3: DLPack dtype field doesn't match a Nucleor numeric type. Check RFC-0010 §3.4 for the supported codes.
column4: RFC-0010 §3.4 — DLPack dtype is a (code, bits, lanes) triple. Code 0=Int, 1=UInt, 2=Float, 3=BFloat, 4=Complex, 5=Bool. The supplied combination doesn't map to a Nucleor numeric type.

column3: Tensor's runtime shape doesn't match the static shape declared on the import side. Reshape upstream or relax the static shape.
column4: RFC-0010 §3.2 — bind sites can carry static shapes via Tensor<Shape>. The runtime-discovered shape must agree, or upstream must reshape.

column2: Non-contiguous tensor and no copy requested
column3: DLPack tensor's strides don't match a contiguous layout. Pass copy_on_import=true or contiguify upstream.
column4: RFC-0010 §3.5 — DLPack tensors expose strides; if not contiguous and copy_on_import is false, Nucleor refuses (a copy would be unexpected). Either pass copy_on_import=true or contiguify upstream (np.ascontiguousarray, .contiguous(), etc.).

column3: DLPack ABI version on the wire is older than this build supports. Upgrade the producer.
column4: RFC-0010 §3.1 — DLPack's struct layout has versioned. The producer is on an older ABI than this Nucleor build. Upgrade the producer.

column3: #[cxx_include] points at a header that doesn't resolve under any --include-path. Add the path or relocate the header.
column4: RFC-0011 §3.1 — #[cxx_include(\"...\")] resolves under --include-path / NUCLEOR_CXX_INCLUDE_PATH. Add the path or move the header.

column2: Type mismatch between Nucleor decl and C++ source
column3: The Nucleor extern \"C++\" decl's signature doesn't match the libclang-extracted signature from the header. Update one to match the other.
column4: RFC-0011 §3.3 — nuc-cxx parses the C++ header with libclang and compares the extracted signature with the Nucleor extern \"C++\" declaration. Mismatches must be reconciled in one direction.

column3: std::function is type-erased dispatch; #[no_dyn] forbids it. Refactor to a concrete callable type or opt out with #[allow(no_dyn)].
column4: RFC-0011 §3.2 — std::function is type-erased and uses dynamic dispatch (typically allocating a heap functor). #[no_dyn] forbids both. Replace with a concrete callable or opt out at the call site.

column3: Types crossing the C++ bridge must have stable layouts. Add #[repr(C)] to the struct or wrap it.
column4: RFC-0011 §3.1 — types crossing the bridge must have layout the C++ side can rely on. Add #[repr(C)] to make the layout C-stable.

column3: C++ exceptions cannot unwind through a Nucleor frame. Wrap the C++ call site with try/catch and convert to Result<T, CxxError>.
column4: RFC-0011 §5 — Nucleor frames don't unwind through C++ exceptions; the runtime intentionally aborts on uncaught C++ exceptions to preserve safety. Wrap the C++ call site in a try/catch that converts to Result<T, CxxError>.

column3: nuc-bindgen could not locate the C header. Add --include-path or fix the spelling in the bindgen.toml.
column4: RFC-0012 §3.1 — bindgen.toml's [headers] section lists C headers; each must resolve under --include-path. Either add the path or fix the spelling.

column3: libclang failed to parse the header. Common causes: missing -D defines, missing system headers, or C++ syntax in a .h file. Pass --extra-clang-arg to bindgen.
column4: RFC-0012 §4 — libclang emitted parse errors. Common causes: missing #defines, missing system headers (add a sysroot), or C++ syntax in a .h file. Pass --extra-clang-arg='-D...' or '-isystem...'.

column3: C type has no Nucleor analog (e.g., GCC vector extensions, _Complex). Add a manual binding or skip with bindgen.toml's [skip] section.
column4: RFC-0012 §3.2 — some C types have no Nucleor analog (GCC vector extensions, _Complex, __int128 on 32-bit targets). Either add a manual wrapper or skip the symbol with bindgen.toml [skip].

column3: Header declares `struct foo;` but never defines it. Either #include the definition or mark the type opaque in bindgen.toml.
column4: RFC-0012 §3.2 — `struct foo;` with no struct definition leaves the type opaque. Either #include the file that defines it (so libclang can extract the layout) or mark it opaque in bindgen.toml [opaque] (compiler will treat it as a void* handle).

column3: Two #include paths produced different definitions of the same symbol. Resolve by --keep-only or by reorganizing the include order.
column4: RFC-0012 — duplicate symbol from two #include paths. Resolve via [keep_only] in bindgen.toml or by reordering includes so the canonical definition wins.

column2: No path from A to B in any imported URDF
column3: RFC-0013 verifies frame chains at compile time. The compiler couldn't find a transform path between the two named frames in any URDF on the import path.
column4: RFC-0013 §3.2 — frame chain compile-time check. The compiler walks every imported URDF and could not find a transform path between the two named frames. Either import a URDF that connects them or add a #[urdf_attach] joint.

column2: A and B in different URDFs without #[urdf_attach]
column3: Two frames belong to separate URDF trees. Bridge them with #[urdf_attach(parent, child)] to declare the joint, or import a unified URDF.
column4: RFC-0013 §3.3 — multiple URDF imports produce disjoint trees. #[urdf_attach(parent_frame, child_frame)] declares the joint that bridges them; without it the compiler refuses cross-tree transforms.

column3: URDF parser detected a cycle (e.g. base_link → arm_link → base_link). The kinematic graph must be a tree.
column4: RFC-0013 — the kinematic graph must be a DAG (rooted at base_link). A cycle suggests either a malformed URDF or two #[urdf_attach] joints that close a loop. Remove one of the bridging joints.

column3: #[urdf_load(\"...\")] points to a missing file. Check working directory and import paths.
column4: RFC-0013 §3.1 — #[urdf_load(\"path/to/robot.urdf\")] resolves relative to the source file's directory. Check the path and ensure the URDF is in source control or a known asset dir.

column3: URDF XML failed to parse. Common issues: missing <robot> root, malformed <joint> attributes, mismatched origin tags.
column4: RFC-0013 §3.1 — URDF parser uses minixml; common parse errors include missing <robot> root, malformed <joint type=\"...\"> attributes, mismatched origin tags, and unsupported plugin tags. Validate the URDF with `urdf-validator` first.

column3: Joint angle/displacement passed to lookup() exceeds the URDF-declared joint limit. Clamp upstream or relax the limit in the URDF.
column4: RFC-0013 §3.4 — joint limits are declared in the URDF as <limit lower upper effort velocity/>. lookup() with an out-of-range angle/displacement is rejected. Clamp upstream or relax the URDF limit if mechanically valid.

column2: Max-depth analysis cannot bound recursive path
column3: The RFC-0014 analyzer found recursion but could not prove a finite bound. Use a visible counter parameter, entry guard, and a positive counter increment; mark callback parameters #[no_recurse] only when they cannot recurse into the max_depth region.
column4: RFC-0014 structural proof requires a visible counter and a guard. Unmarked callback paths, missing guards, or non-positive/non-literal recursive updates are rejected conservatively.

column3: The analyzer proved a finite recursion depth, but that depth is larger than the declared #[max_depth = N].
column4: RFC-0014 compared the proven guard depth with the declared N and found the code needs more stack frames than the annotation allows. Raise N or reduce the recursion depth.

column3: A mutually-recursive cycle has incompatible or unproven #[max_depth] bounds. Runtime overrun checks also report this code when a counter exceeds N.
column4: RFC-0014 SCC analysis found a cycle whose member bounds do not compose. Give every function in the cycle compatible guards/bounds or refactor through a single trampoline.

column3: `#[max_depth]` must use a positive integer literal and apply directly to a fn declaration.
column4: RFC-0014 only accepts fn-level #[max_depth = N] / #[max_depth(N)] with a positive integer literal. Other placements and symbolic values are rejected.

column3: Sum of (max_depth_i * estimated_frame_size_i) along a recursion chain exceeds the project's stack budget.
column4: RFC-0014 stack-budget check multiplies declared depth by estimated frame size. Reduce locals/frame size, reduce N, or convert recursion to iteration.

column2: Generated law check failed, declared law has unsupported arity, or canonical form lacks a shipped bounded checker
column3: `nuc test --check-laws` generated a bounded integer check for a low-risk @law annotation and the check failed, or the declared law has unsupported arity for the annotated function. The shipped checker covers commutative, associative, identity, absorbing, idempotent, involution, distributive_over, and unary inverse forms (inverse round-trips `f(g(a)) == a` and `g(f(a)) == a` at four bounded sample integers). Fusion generation, Arbitrary-driven broad property tests, float tolerance handling, and SMT proof obligations remain future RFC-0031 phases and fail closed instead of being silently accepted.
column4: `nuc test --check-laws` generated a bounded integer check for a low-risk @law annotation and found a counterexample, or the declaration is arity-incompatible with the annotated function (or, for `inverse = g`, the partner name is missing). The checker currently covers commutative, associative, identity, absorbing, idempotent, involution, distributive_over, and unary inverse forms; broader random Arbitrary generation, fusion generation, float tolerance handling, and cert-profile SMT proofs remain queued.

column2: SMT disproves law (RESERVED — Phase 3 not shipped)
column3: RESERVED diagnostic. Phase 3 of RFC-0031 will route @law through Z3/CVC5 SMT proof under --profile=cert. Phase 1 (v0.8.265) does not run any solver; LAW-002 is reserved for future emission.
column4: RESERVED. Phase 3 of RFC-0031 will route @law through Z3/CVC5 SMT proof under --profile=cert. As of v0.8.265 (Phase 1) no solver runs; LAW-002 is reserved for future emission.

column2: Law cited but optimizer cannot use it (RESERVED — Phase 2 not shipped)
column3: RESERVED diagnostic. Phase 2 of RFC-0031 will pattern-match @law citations during optimizer pass; today the law-rewrite pass is a metadata-only no-op (v0.8.265). LAW-003 is reserved for the rewrite pass once it has real semantics.
